title: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics
summary: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.

title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.

title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
summary: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.
comment: 5 pages. 2 figues. Extended version of a paper accepted to the AAAI-27 Demonstrations Program. Code: https://github.com/waldiez/wactorz

title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
summary: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. Project page: https://cmu-l3.github.io/kernel-shift/

title: Detectable Epistemic Attack Layers: A Coverage Theorem and Standardized Harness for Conversation-History Integrity
summary: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. All protocols and acceptance criteria are pre-registered; the stack and harness are released.
comment: 36 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Harness, protocol texts, and pre-registration: https://github.com/fahrellgiovanny/conversation-history-integrity

title: Deep Negative Binomial Autoregression for Sparse Spatio-Temporal Counts: Estimation and Predictive Distribution Bounds
summary: We study estimation and probabilistic forecasting for sparse, overdispersed count panels using DeepNB-STAR, a negative binomial autoregression whose log-mean and log-size are outputs of a deep ReLU network of temporal and neighboring summaries of the past, fitted by maximum likelihood. We prove an oracle inequality for the Hellinger risk along the observed trajectory without mixing assumptions, rates governed by compositional smoothness with a matching lower bound for a Hölder subclass, geometric absolute regularity, and bounds on the error of h-step predictive distributions of order h^{1/2} times the root estimation risk plus a Monte Carlo term. All results hold for a size that depends on the covariates, and the estimation bounds hold under arbitrary dependence between sites, with the number of time points as sample size. On four Japanese surveillance panels, DeepNB-STAR has a weighted interval score 0.6% to 1.0% below that of a three-member ensemble of Temporal Fusion Transformers on every panel, distinguishable from zero only on the held-out panel. Fitted mean and size functions are reported with exploratory bootstrap intervals. Nominal 95% prediction intervals for national totals cover only 81% to 92% of weeks: the joint predictive law, unlike the estimator, relies on conditional independence across sites.
comment: 71 pages (50-page paper followed by a 21-page supplement), 5 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Machine Learning Research. Code, data and a demonstration notebook: https://github.com/hhuang45/DeepNB-STAR

title: DriveOddsBench: Are Driving Video World Models Aligned with Real-World Odds?
summary: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the real outcome among them is uniform in every history, so pooled ranks test them without probability labels. Second, one validated instrument reads the same quantities, such as the lead-vehicle gap and the ego motion, from the generated futures and from the real future, which first passes through the world model's autoencoder so that both are read alike. Third, all confirmatory analyses were frozen before any test clip was measured. We test eleven general and driving world models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories in five scenario families, with 35,200 generated futures. None is aligned, and every model underestimates its uncertainty. The real outcome falls outside the range of all 16 samples in 28-61% of cases instead of the 11.8% expected under the real distribution. Five models are significantly skewed, in opposite directions, and the largest errors are in the ego motion. Nine models beat climatology without being aligned, and among these models neither type nor scale predicts which comes closest.
comment: 22 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/DriveOddsBench-page/ Code: https://github.com/hhjj233/DriveOddsBench

title: Similarity-Constrained Reweighting for Complex Query Answering on Knowledge Graphs
summary: Machine learning models for Complex Query Answering (CQA) on knowledge graphs estimate the likelihood of answers that are not reachable via direct traversal. Recent work has proposed extending such queries with soft entity constraints, which require the target variable to be similar or dissimilar to specified sets of entities. We study a more general formulation where similarity constraints are specified on an arbitrary variable in a query, and introduce SCORE: a computationally efficient and interpretable method for incorporating similarity constraints on an arbitrary variable of a query. SCORE is based on a lightweight and interpretable score adjustment function that only requires tuning two hyperparameters on a validation set. Our experiments show that SCORE effectively incorporates preferences while maintaining strong query answering performance. It significantly improves ranking quality when constraints apply to the target variable and performs effectively in the more general case involving constraints on intermediate variables, and its performance remains robust when applied to several existing methods for CQA. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/dfdazac/score.

title: Ego-HMB: Human Motion Bridging from Egocentric Images via A Motion Bridge Diffusion Model
summary: We introduce Egocentric Human Motion Bridging, a task that generates a coherent 3D human motion sequence from two endpoint egocentric images. Unlike conventional motion in-betweening, which requires structured 3D endpoint poses, this setting uses raw first-person observations available from wearable devices in VR/AR and robotics. It presents challenges due to viewpoint variations, partial body visibility, and temporal ambiguity under cross-modal endpoint constraints. To address these challenges, we propose Ego-HMB, a unified diffusion-based framework that learns endpoint pose estimation and temporally consistent motion infilling within a single model through two training stages. First, Egocentric-to-Canonical Pretraining uses a hierarchical curriculum with progressively increasing temporal spans to strengthen endpoint pose priors. Second, Motion Bridge Diffusion Training incorporates endpoint and physics awareness, diffusing from neighboring poses to promote temporal continuity while preserving global endpoint constraints. Extensive experiments compare our approach with one-stage methods that directly generate motion from two egocentric images and two-stage pipelines that combine endpoint pose estimation with motion interpolation. Ego-HMB consistently outperforms these baselines in endpoint accuracy and motion generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/gaogehan/Ego-HMB.

title: Towards Global Counterfactual-Based Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph Counterfactual Explanations (GCEs) have emerged as an effective approach for interpreting Graph Neural Network (GNN) predictions by identifying minimal graph modifications needed to change predictions. However, existing methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) They rely on a post-hoc explanation paradigm, where a separate explainer is trained after the GNN. This sequential optimization prevents the explainer from leveraging how the GNN learned its representations, often resulting in lower-quality explanations. (2) They are largely local, generating counterfactual explanations only for individual samples. Consequently, they fail to capture generalizable patterns across the data distribution, a crucial gap for applications like drug discovery, where global principles enable systematic decision-making across thousands of cases. To address these limitations, we propose GCSGNN (Global Counterfactual-based Self-explainable GNN), a unified framework that integrates counterfactual generation into the GNN architecture, encouraging explanations that faithfully reflect the model's decision-making process. Beyond local explanations, GCSGNN discovers shared latent patterns influencing predictions across graphs, yielding global (i.e., model-level) counterfactual explanations. We further introduce an efficient latent-space counterfactual mechanism that avoids the combinatorial complexity of discrete graph manipulation, enabling scalable discovery of generalizable modification patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GCSGNN outperforms existing methods in generating effective counterfactual explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/gcsgnn.

title: A Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Color Normalization Methods in Histopathology: Nuclei Preservation, Artifact Sensitivity, Background Fidelity, and Downstream Performanc
summary: Deep learning models for nuclei detection and classification may generalize poorly across medical centers because of variations in staining and scanning. Although color normalization aims to reduce these variations, its effects on nuclear structure, background preservation, artifact sensitivity, and nuclei detection and classification performance have not been systematically evaluated. We present a procedure to benchmark 11 classical and deep learning normalization methods using 7 public and private nuclei datasets. Additionally, we investigate the effect of 7 input color spaces. The normalization methods differed in their effects on nuclear structure, background, and sensitivity to artifacts. However, detection and classification performance varied more across datasets than across normalization methods, and the input color space had limited influence. No single method performed best on all criteria, and image-level metrics did not reliably predict downstream performance, highlighting the need for nuclei- and structure-aware normalization methods. To support this work, we introduce WSI Quality Control and Normalization (WSI-QCN), a publicly available pipeline for robust whole-slide image quality assessment and color normalization; the source code is available on GitHub.

title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
summary: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.
comment: 26 pages. Lang Lin, Tianyu Chen, Yi Gu, Yang Zhao, Xinran Song and Xinyang Liu contributed equally. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM ; media: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Swindl/S1Arena-MM

title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
summary: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
summary: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.
comment: Code and data are available on the project page: https://yingheng-wang.com/DeepDOSReasoner/

title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models
summary: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.

title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
summary: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

title: PAWP-TTS: Phoneme-Aware Weight Programming for Compact Bilingual English-Nepali Speech Synthesis
summary: This paper presents PAWP-TTS, a compact non-autoregressive text-to-speech system for English, Nepali, and English-Nepali code-mixed speech at 24 kHz, with no language model at inference. Deterministic pronunciation knowledge lives in a rule- and lexicon-based bilingual frontend that preserves native Nepali contrasts and avoids Hindi phonology, so the network only models acoustics. Counting every learned inference tensor, including the waveform decoder, PAWP-1.5M (1,490,390 parameters, 5.98 MB) reaches 1.50% English and 1.75% Nepali character error rate under a single ASR recognizer, and 5.04% / 4.02% Nepali / English phoneme error rate (PER) on 600 untouched test utterances. Decoder-centric 281K-parameter models (1.1 MB) stay intelligible across three independent seeds, with equal-budget dense models (5.53 +/- 0.08% NE, 5.34 +/- 0.28% EN PER) outperforming K=2 cross-layer shared-basis models (6.35 +/- 0.11% NE, 6.57 +/- 0.47% EN PER). Fixing a frontend/label version mismatch nearly halved Nepali PER, more than any architectural or weight-level change. The paper then studies weight-space programming: inspection-guided, zero-training weight edits. Under strict controls (validation-only selection, one-shot test, paired bootstrap, matched random and same-parameter gradient baselines), edits show real selectivity (27:1 on word-boundary pauses with 96 weights; zero cross-lingual collateral inside language-gated residuals) but no accuracy gain beyond controls. Two apparent targets proved to be label or phonology artifacts. Code, ONNX graphs, and CC BY 4.0 weights are released.
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Code: https://github.com/Firojpaudel/PAWP_TTS | Audio Demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/Firoj112/pawp-tts-demo | Models: https://huggingface.co/Firoj112/pawp-tts-1.5m and https://huggingface.co/Firoj112/pawp-tts-300k

title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
summary: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. 41 pages, 6 figures. Project website: https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/

title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
summary: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

title: Endpoint-Conditioned Process Value: What an Endpoint-Blind Process Score Adds Once Terminal Status and Cost Are Known
summary: Trajectory metrics promise information beyond final-answer accuracy, but no one has measured what a process score adds once an evaluation knows the outcome and the cost. We build that comparison: a sealed consequence needing an artifact neither agent nor judge ever sees, an operational baseline of terminal status and cost, and judge scale and evidence access as experimental factors. On 1,255 trajectories over 158 test-generation tasks in 7 Python repositories, the answer is gated on the judge. Four judges from 4B to 14B, one reasoning before scoring, add nothing an interval separates from zero; a Qwen3 32B judge on identical trajectories adds +0.050 AUC (95% CI [+0.020, +0.081]) and survives a refitting bootstrap ([+0.013, +0.095]). Most of what it adds is recoverable from eight behavioural counters, so a harness should log them (the judge adds +0.020 beyond them). What the judge is shown moves it further: disclosing the terminal verdict inflates its standalone discrimination by +0.103, while reference disclosure and tool-output redaction move it by nothing an interval separates from zero. A process metric reported without the judge's scale and evidence access does not identify a quantity. We release the protocol, the sealed-endpoint harness, and all trajectories.

title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
summary: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, Sánchez, Feijóo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for Sánchez and Feijóo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare Sánchez and right personas spare Feijóo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.

title: CT-Navigator: Towards Interpretable and Generalizable CT Understanding through Agentic Perception and Tool-Invocation
summary: Clinical computed tomography (CT) interpretation inherently requires progressive visual exploration, where radiologists navigate from whole scans to individual slices and regions of interest and interact with external tools when necessary. However, existing 3D medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically connect a specialized 3D visual encoder to a language model, without fully leveraging the native 2D visual and agentic capabilities of generalist MLLMs. Trained on large-scale one-hop CT instruction-following data, these models also have limited ability to perform iterative reasoning and explicitly ground their conclusions in visual evidence, limiting their support for traceable CT interpretation. To solve these problems, we propose \textbf{agentic perception} as an alternative paradigm inspired by radiologists' interpretation workflows. We introduce \textbf{CT-Navigator}, a framework that harnesses generalist MLLMs' 2D visual and agentic capabilities to progressively ground CT interpretation in explicit, traceable visual evidence through hierarchical visual exploration and radiology tool invocation. To build these capabilities, we curate 8,904 visual chain-of-thought (V-CoT) trajectories for cold-start agentic supervised fine-tuning. We then optimize the policy through reinforcement learning on 33,219 questions, with data selection and dynamic rollout sampling prioritizing informative learning signals. Finally, we introduce CTNavi-Bench, a 3D CT visual question answering benchmark comprising 7,000 questions spanning anatomical regions throughout the human body. CT-Navigator achieves 79.50\% accuracy on CTNavi-Bench, surpassing the strongest baseline by 17.59\%, and demonstrates strong generalization across three external CT benchmarks. The code, model, and benchmark will be released on \href{https://github.com/fyb99/ct_navigator}{GitHub}.

title: Perplexity and Intelligence
summary: How perplexity measures progress in AI models, and why it could help developers establish a shared approach to evaluating emerging capabilities.

title: Align the Pair, Not the Sample: Representation Alignment for Faster and Better One-Step Generators
summary: Representation alignment markedly accelerates diffusion training, but one-step generators raise a question that diffusion does not: \emph{which training path should receive the loss?} A one-step generator sees two kinds of inputs. Corrupted real images come with their clean counterpart, which provides an instance-paired target. Samples generated from pure noise have no corresponding real image, yet this is where the final model operates. We study this question on Priming, which trains one-step generators from scratch by reconstructing corrupted images and then matching feature distributions with optimal transport. Aligning the generative path, the natural choice, collapses recall ($0.45\!\to\!0.15$--$0.25$) in all 17 configurations we test, including five target constructions and loss weights down to $0.05$. Aligning the paired reconstruction path with a frozen DINOv2 encoder instead helps in every setting we test. A short analysis explains this asymmetry: when the target carries no instance information about the input, the optimal aligned feature is constant within each class, so the loss pulls samples toward class prototypes. A control confirms this: aligning the paired path to a random same-class image instead of the input's own image removes most of the gain. Inside the generator, paired-path alignment creates an interface block through which post-training routes noise, and the image semantics carried through it predict sample quality across 16 models. The resulting recipe, \method, accelerates \emph{both} training stages on ImageNet $256\!\times\!256$: it matches the 160-epoch baseline with $2\times$ fewer priming epochs, surpasses its final quality with $4\times$ fewer post-training updates, and lowers FID to 1.30 (B) and 1.155 (L) at the standard budget. A joint single-stage variant trains native one-step generators and reaches FID 1.22 with 115M parameters.

title: Loop-Count Schedules in Looped Transformers: An Empirical Study
summary: Looped transformers apply one block of layers several times with shared weights, trading parameters for repeated computation. We study how the schedule of the loop iteration count R during training determines whether each extra pass acts as a full layer or as a small correction, using a controlled ladder of 46M-110M-parameter models trained on 2B tokens with learned residual gates on every loop pass and three schedules: R fixed to 2, R sampled uniformly from {1,...,6}, and R sampled from {2,3,4}. We find that the lower bound of the sampling range is the decisive choice. If the sampled range includes R=1, so that some training steps run the block only once and compute the loss on that single pass, the gates collapse to 0.1-0.5 and each additional pass becomes a small correction to the first; if the range starts at R=2, so that every training step runs the block at least twice, the gates stay at 0.6-0.9 and each pass keeps the strength of a full layer, while the model can still be run at any R from 2 up to twice the largest trained value with validation loss within a few hundredths of a nat of its best. The {2, 3, 4} schedule gives the best looped model, 2.909 nats against 2.951 for the parameter-matched plain model, and degrades by only 0.038 nats when run at twice its trained depth. We further show that under a fixed R the direction of the residual stream converges geometrically beyond the trained depth while the loss diverges, which refines a recent finding that static-depth training does not converge, and that reusing the first pass's keys and values on later passes costs 0.01-0.03 nats in every regime while making the per-token iteration uniformly contractive and halving the inference cache. The loop recovers about a third of what real depth provides at equal parameters. The code, trained weights, and per-token traces are released.

title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
summary: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall
summary: An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.

title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
summary: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

title: Why flattening the P-value histogram works: a theory of the standard-deviation optimization in tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction
summary: Background: Tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction (TD-based UFE) selects genes by attributing P-values to the components of a gene singular vector under a null normal distribution. The standard deviation sigma of this distribution is unknown and is chosen so that the histogram of the P-values of the genes that are not selected becomes as flat as possible. This heuristic has worked well in practice but has had no theoretical justification. Results: We prove, for a model of signal, mean expression and noise, that the higher-order singular value decomposition has a component that reproduces the experimental design, that the components of its gene singular vector belonging to background genes are approximately normal with standard deviation sigma_0 = sqrt(d)/s, where d is the noise variance and s the singular value, and that signal genes separate from the background even when they form a positive fraction of all genes. We derive the limit of the objective function of the flattening and prove, by a computer-assisted argument based on interval arithmetic, that for 100 histogram bins, Benjamini-Hochberg level 0.01 and every fraction of background genes between 0.1 and 0.99, the limit has a unique minimizer within 1.1% of sigma_0. We formalize the practice of taking the valley to the right of the peak of the objective as a maximum-drop rule and prove that the resulting estimator is consistent up to this bounded bias. Conclusions: Flattening the P-value histogram estimates the noise level of the background genes, with a small and bounded systematic bias, provided that the signals are strong enough to be detected individually and that the noise variances of background genes are nearly equal.

title: Scenario Compliant Indoor Pedestrian Trajectory Reconstruction from Partial Observation
summary: Pedestrian trajectory reconstruction is vital for applications ranging from security surveillance to indoor navigation. While existing probabilistic and generative frameworks have shown success in outdoor GPS-based trajectory imputation, they often fail in indoor settings where movement is strictly governed by dense geometric constraints such as walls and corridors. Standard models typically treat trajectories as unconstrained coordinate sequences, leading to physically infeasible paths with high collision rates. To address this, we propose a map-conditioned generative framework based on conditional diffusion models. Our approach explicitly integrates dense scenario maps as structured spatial inputs via a CNN-based encoder, allowing environmental geometry to guide the iterative denoising process. Furthermore, we employ an endpoint-aware mechanism by embedding observations (start and end points) directly into the scenario map, providing critical spatial anchors through image-level features. Experiments on simulated indoor trajectories and the real-world Shopper trajectory dataset, with three training seeds, show that our method achieves the lowest errors among the compared generative methods. Scene conditioning reduces the collision and invalid rates by 19\% and 46\% on the simulated dataset, whereas on real shopper data the gains are consistent but small, mainly because the model rarely learns to route around obstacles between the endpoints. Compared with a shortest-path planner, which never collides, our method better captures the variability of real motion (31\% lower CRPS), but the timing of stops is reconstructed only partially. These results show that explicit environmental context improves physical consistency, while reconstructing realistic human motion in real indoor spaces remains challenging. Our code is available at https://github.com/dang-qi/trajectory_reconstruction

title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
summary: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.

title: loopxDINO: Dense Visual Prediction via Iterative Latent Reasoning
summary: Standard dense visual prediction architectures scale representation capacity by stacking deep feedforward decoders (6-16 transformer layers with 50M-200M parameters). This explicit layer stacking brings substantial activation memory overhead during backpropagation, requires high off-chip memory bandwidth for non-tied weights, and uses static computational allocation that cannot adapt to spatial image complexity. We propose loopxDINO, which replaces physical decoder depth with iterative latent reasoning. It has two decoupled components: (1) a frozen DINOv2-Base backbone extracting spatial features in one forward pass and caching static Key-Value representations in GPU memory; (2) a compact weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (7.96M core, 14.85M total trainable parameters) that recurrently updates queries across T iterations. Recurrence is stabilized by step-conditioned adaLN, LayerNorm-based hyper-ellipsoid manifold regularization, and learnable residual contraction damping. Intermediate mask predictions are fed back as spatial attention biases to guide queries toward ambiguous contours with no extra parameters. On Pascal VOC 2012 semantic segmentation with a single RTX 5060 Ti 16GB GPU, loopxDINO (T=2) achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU. It outperforms 6-layer DINO-Trans6L (54.06M params) by +1.09% mIoU and +7.41% Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer parameters. Compared to 4-layer DINO-FCN4L probe (2.43M params, 83.82% mIoU), loopxDINO improves boundary delineation by +6.43% bIoU and occlusion resilience by +6.76% mIoU (60% patch masking). With Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), it reaches 87.3 FPS and retains 29.64% mIoU under 60% occlusion (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L). Source code, pre-trained weights and evaluation suites are open-sourced under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/loopxDINO/loopxDINO

title: ContinuLoc: Continuous Pose Inference over Neural Fields for UAV Geo-Localization
summary: Cross-view UAV geo-localization involves three design choices: how to represent the UAV observation, how to represent the geo-referenced map, and how to infer pose from their interaction. The dominant paradigm organizes the map as a discretized 2DoF candidate library, coupling map representation to pose inference and thus bounding spatial localization precision by candidate sampling resolution. We decouple map representation from pose inference by encoding the geo-referenced map as a continuously queryable semantic neural field, enabling localization to be formulated as explicit optimization over a continuous 4DoF pose space parameterized by 2D ground position, in-plane heading, and viewing scale. Pose hypotheses are evaluated on demand using global descriptors in a shared semantic feature space, bypassing the sampling bottleneck of retrieval. We learn 4DoF pose-sensitive visual representations under full 4DoF supervision provided by ContinuScenes, a multi-city benchmark with dense near-nadir UAV imagery and complete pose annotations. Inference proceeds hierarchically, progressing from broad pose-space coverage to adaptive concentration on high-compatibility regions. Experiments demonstrate substantial gains over representative localization paradigms under progressively stricter 4DoF accuracy criteria. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhouWeikun/ContinuLoc/

title: SKIA: Spatial-Knowledge Informed Attention for Robust Remote Photoplethysmography under Lower-Face Motion Artifacts
summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables contactless physiological monitoring from facial videos, but facial motion, particularly mouth and jaw movements during cognitive and communicative tasks, can severely degrade signal reconstruction. We present SKIA, a lightweight, mask-guided framework that suppresses motion-prone lower-face regions while preserving physiological cues from the forehead and cheeks. Using the UBFC-rPPG benchmark, we first investigate static lower-face suppression in the classical CHROM pipeline. Static masking improves waveform Pearson correlation from 0.3507 to 0.4166 (p < 0.001) and reduces heart-rate mean absolute error (MAE) from 33.50 to 23.44 bpm. Building on this finding, we introduce SKIA-Net, a compact spatiotemporal architecture that combines raw facial frames, statically masked representations, and temporal motion differences to reconstruct blood volume pulse (BVP) waveforms. The full model achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.7522 and a heart-rate MAE of 3.73 bpm on UBFC-rPPG, outperforming single-stream variants. Ablation studies show that the static mask provides complementary information to raw appearance and that static anatomical priors outperform the tested dynamic optical-flow-based masking strategy. These results suggest that spatially informed, temporally stable masking can improve motion-robust rPPG estimation. Code: https://github.com/lee-vtruong/SKIA-rPPG

title: Where Does Personalization Reside in Photo Editing? Evidence from One Photographer's Lightroom History
summary: Personalized photo-editing systems must infer both a photographer's recurring preferences and the intent of a particular shoot, yet these signals are rarely evaluated separately. We study interpretable Lightroom adjustments in a longitudinal, private dataset of 3,193 edited photographs from 41 catalogs by one professional photographer, with holdouts formed at the batch level. We compare absolute and prior-relative targets, image-conditioned predictors, and estimators that receive a small set of edits from the target batch. Residual prediction improves validation error, but its advantage on held-out batches is small and not significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap (0.592 vs 0.582 EV exposure MAE). In a batch-shared protocol, closed-form shrinkage using 4, 8, or 16 same-batch anchors reaches 0.466, 0.457, or 0.453 EV with the best estimator at each k, compared with 0.586-0.592 EV for the prior-only baseline; the paired reductions are significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap. Learned anchor-conditioned heads do not improve on this closed-form estimator, and a negative-trained prior already yields a low cold-image false-edit rate, leaving little benefit for an additional gate. The recommended estimator is closed-form and auditable, and it requires only a handful of same-batch edits. A render-space check against 383 native Lightroom exports reproduces the ranking: at k=8, online EB lowers Delta E00 against the prior by 0.41 (p=0.042), and the photographer's true parameters lower it by 0.78 (p=0.034). An appendix extends the action space from six to thirteen global controls: a same-batch median look lowers rendered chroma toward the export, while a per-photograph residual head again fails to transfer. The study is limited to one photographer and does not claim that slider accuracy measures aesthetic preference.

title: HorizonFlow: Few-Step Video Distillation in 600 Iterations
summary: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) enables fast video generation by distilling a multi-step teacher into a few-step student. However, DMD-based methods often suffer from unnatural motion and costly training. We trace these limitations to the DMD gradient, which jointly optimizes appearance, layout, and motion without distinguishing their learning dynamics. Its static component, which carries appearance and layout, has a much higher signal-to-noise ratio than its motion component. As a result, per-frame quality converges within a few hundred iterations, whereas motion lags far behind. Beyond being noisy, the gradient also lacks two signals. (1) Video VAEs encode several frames into one latent frame (four in Wan2.1), and the gradient provides little guidance for spreading motion over these frames, causing periodic stutter. (2) DMD does not constrain the final sampling step to preserve the layout set by earlier steps, so objects merge and drift once the video moves. We propose HorizonFlow, which decouples the correction of motion from that of layout. It keeps the DMD loss and only shifts its regression target, with one training-only correction in the motion component and one in the orthogonal layout component. Chunk Evenness addresses (1) by spreading the motion of each latent chunk evenly over its frames, and Semantic Commitment addresses (2) by anchoring the coarse layout to the teacher's completion of the student's last step. In only 600 iterations, HorizonFlow distills Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B into a 4-step model using 8.4k training samples, 4.6-304$\times$ fewer than prior work. On VBench, HorizonFlow outperforms all released few-step Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B models. The same recipe transfers to Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B, where our student outperforms NVIDIA's distilled model. Code: https://github.com/XIANGLONGGUO/HorizonFlow-repo

title: Automatic Construction of Persian E-Commerce Dialogue Datasets for Conversational Product Search
summary: Conversational product search lets users find products through a multi-turn dialogue instead of a single keyword query, but Persian lacks the large conversational datasets needed to train and evaluate such systems; existing Persian e-commerce dialogue resources cover few categories and small catalogs. We present a framework that builds such a dataset automatically from a real e-commerce catalog and release the resulting dataset. The framework crawls 12,926 products in seven categories of the Digikala marketplace, groups them into 170 semantically coherent clusters, and selects the question the assistant asks at every turn with the Regularized Partition Balance (RPB) score. The RPB score accounts for feature coverage, the probability that the user can answer and the number of values, and generalizes entropy-based question selection. An LLM then verbalizes each question plan into a natural Persian dialogue. In a simulation on the full catalog, the RPB score needs 0.11 fewer turns than the strongest entropy baseline when the difficulty of answering differs between features, and is practically equivalent to it when it does not. Using only a free LLM API, we generated 1,000 requirement-driven dialogues covering all 170 clusters, with turn-level feature annotations; automatic checks and an LLM judge confirm their consistency with the catalog, while their realism is lower than that of the first, GPT-4o-generated version. Code and data are publicly available.

title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
summary: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. We build a 640-task benchmark with three test sets (larger circuits, an unseen circuit family, an unseen Qiskit coding style) and a QuantumKatas regression probe, and we test the evaluator before training. Measurement counts miss every phase-only error; a surface rule-based translator solves two of three original splits (text substitution); a converter that executes the Qiskit input and maps the circuit solves all 640 tasks -- so the benchmark measures source-level translation, not whether a circuit can be ported after running it. No base model emits a valid CUDA-Q kernel zero-shot. On Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, LoRA reaches 83.9%, tying a 4-shot prompt (83.1%), but generalizes worse to unseen style (48.5% vs. 65.5%) and cuts QuantumKatas from 23.8% to 8.9%; on Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, LoRA beats the prompt overall (92.0% vs. 82.8%) and on unseen style (78.5% vs. 65.0%), and on the 1.5B model as well, so whether fine-tuning pays off depends on the base model, while the Qiskit regression appears in all three. Mixing two replay formats is the best mitigation trade-off (84.4% translation, Katas 21.5%). On 48 parametric functions that must become kernels with arguments -- where executing the input cannot yield a parametric kernel -- models reach up to 83%; on 27 real QED-C kernels, every model scores 0%. Language models can do source-level translation of simple parametric code, but not yet of real programs.

title: Contact Harness: Enabling VLM Agents to Perform Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force and tactile feedback provide complementary information, but their semantic ambiguity makes them difficult for agents to use directly. These signals must be interpreted according to their physical meaning, together with task phase and visual evidence. We propose Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions. A compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback. The framework requires no model fine-tuning, task demonstrations, or simulation training. We conduct zero-shot real-robot evaluations using GPT-6 Astra on Rokae and Franka robots. With a single prompt skill, Contact Harness achieves a full-insertion rate of 90.7% across 15 connector types, with further evaluations on a real PC under variations in lighting, background, and position. Across four additional contact-rich tasks, including whiteboard wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting, Contact Harness achieves an average success rate of 100%. On six simulated tasks, Contact Harness reaches 96.7% success, compared with at most 68.3% for pretrained VLA baselines fine-tuned on task demonstrations, showing the potential of agent-based manipulation for contact-rich real-world deployment.

title: Force2Act: A Force-Aware Visuomotor Policy for Generalizable Compliant Robot Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to regulate the force it applies, not only where it moves. Existing force-aware policies learn this force from demonstrations and therefore reproduce the force levels they were trained on, which fails once the interaction demands more force than any demonstration. We present Force2Act, a hybrid force-position policy built on two complementary mechanisms. A global force policy plans the motion and the interaction force once per action chunk, with force represented relative to the measured interaction, so that the planned force scales with the load. Between planning steps, a reactive compliance policy, termed Mixture of Force Experts, identifies at every control step the force expert that governs the interaction and regulates the force through it, so that the contact holds when it changes within a chunk. We further introduce Force2Act-Bench, a simulation benchmark of five contact-rich tasks that gives the community a common and repeatable way to test force-aware policies and measure how well they regulate the interaction force. Force2Act achieves an overall success rate of 93.8%, compared with 77.0% for the strongest baseline, and its reactive regulation reduces the failures on block pivoting from 30 to 10 of 150 trials. On a real robot, Force2Act reaches an average success rate of 94.2% over four tasks, against at most 27.5% for the baselines.

title: Persistent Jailbreak Backdoor Attack
summary: Safety alignment is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) to produce helpful and harmless responses. However, an attacker can plant a jailbreak backdoor in an LLM such that adding a universal trigger word or phrase to a harmful prompt elicits attacker-desired responses. Existing jailbreak backdoor attacks induce distinct behaviors on backdoored inputs and safety samples (harmful prompts paired with refusal responses), making the backdoors susceptible to subsequent safety alignment and advanced defenses. In this paper, we propose a persistent jailbreak backdoor attack that reduces the divergence between clean and trigger-conditioned continuations during LLM decoding, making backdoored samples difficult to distinguish from safety samples. We also introduce a deferred-response mechanism that postpones harmful generations, further disguising the backdoor behavior. We evaluate our attack, PJBack, on eight LLMs from five model families, ranging from 7B to 70B parameters. PJBack achieves an average attack success rate of 93.9% and bypasses all seven evaluated defenses while preserving benign utility. In contrast, five existing backdoor attacks either achieve limited attack success or fail to withstand the evaluated defenses.

title: Social Interaction Breaks Replicate Independence in Controlled-Clone LLM Agents
summary: Multi-agent LLM evaluations and social simulations create many agents from one model and treat them as independent replicates, even after the agents interact. This assumption remains untested with matched controls. We introduce SocCogEval, a controlled-clone assay for Social Cognitive Transfer (SCT). Clones share the base model, system prompt, and decoding parameters and differ only in a private brief, and a factorial protocol separates the brief, 30 rounds of interaction, and initialization noise. On Qwen3-122B-FP8, interaction with the briefs held fixed raises off-topic BFI-10 response-profile drift by $\barΔ=+0.917$ and $+0.912$ in two topically disjoint scenarios (exact $p=0.0008$ and $0.0039$). The drift is larger than under the brief alone, persists under temperature-zero re-probing, and stays positive without typed memory extraction in exploratory tests. Matched solo generation reproduces part of it, and social interaction remains highest. Across five more model variants, every scenario-averaged interaction contrast is positive. Each interacting population is therefore one replicate, and treating its agents as independent requires paired no-interaction controls.

title: Ziv Meets Sumcheck: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Floating-Point LLM Inference
summary: Zero-knowledge proofs can show that a neural network produced a given output without revealing the network, but current systems for language models prove integer approximations of the model rather than the floating-point arithmetic that is actually deployed. Proving floating-point matrix multiplication has been regarded as hard, because rounding after every addition makes the result depend on the order of the additions. We avoid this obstacle by proving the correctly rounded product, in which every dot product is computed exactly and rounded once. This result is independent of the hardware and at least as accurate as standard kernels. We give an interactive proof for this relation whose cost is close to that of integer matrix multiplication, with roughly a thousand times fewer committed values than per-operation floating-point circuits need constraints, extend it to every layer of a transformer, and give a privacy construction for the complete argument whose zero knowledge we prove under explicit hypotheses. We implement the system and prove the full forward pass of GPT-2 small, including all twelve blocks and the output over the whole vocabulary, in 19 minutes on two processor cores; verification takes 21 seconds. The verifier rejects all 236 attacks we tested, and the model's outputs agree with high-precision inference at least as closely as standard 16-bit inference does.

title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
summary: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.

title: Ref2Light: From One Image to Interactive Glasses-Free 3D Characters
summary: Animating character illustrations on light-field displays demands coherent binocular parallax, real-time pose articulation, and fine-grained expression control. However, existing 2D animation and 3D reconstruction pipelines cannot combine these with rapid character switching. We present Ref2Light, a feed-forward framework that maps a single A-pose illustration and continuous pose and expression controls to display-native light-field animation, without per-character 3D reconstruction, rigging, or test-time optimization. Our key insight is to decompose light-field synthesis into static identity, view-dependent parallax, and control-driven articulation. A shared encoder caches multi-scale identity features once per character for rapid switching. A conditional decoder then synthesizes ordered angular anchors from these features via backward texture transport and direct color synthesis. A global-local control scheme deforms the anchors with head-body controls and uses the updated correspondence fields to track facial regions across views for masked local facial refinement. Finally, calibrated differentiable subpixel interlacing converts the anchors into the native panel raster, enabling end-to-end native supervision without rendering all views at full resolution. On held-out VRoid identities, Ref2Light reduces head-body LPIPS by 20.1%-55.6% over 2D and 3D baselines and lowers non-target change MAE in mouth closure by 95.6%-96.5% versus monolithic decoding, while running at 34.0-40.1 FPS for 1440x2560 native rasters on a consumer GPU. Code and demo are in the Supplementary Material.

title: ApexID: Hierarchical Learning for Multi-Species Animal Re-Identification
summary: Animal re-identification (Re-ID) must distinguish individuals across species and capture conditions. We introduce ApexID, a hierarchical SphereFace2-based loss that integrates global identity discrimination with balanced animal-category supervision. Using 132,533 images curated from 19 public datasets, we evaluate three model families and four objectives on four external datasets with observation-aware retrieval protocols. ApexID achieves a dataset-averaged Rank-1 accuracy of 64.89% with ConvNeXt-Small and an mAP of 32.54% with MIEW-ID, outperforming their pretrained reference models. On elephants, a category absent from animal Re-ID training, our ConvNeXt-Small variant achieves the highest retrieval performance among the fourteen evaluated configurations. Scores vary by backbone and dataset, and open-set evaluation reveals remaining discovery challenges. These findings support hierarchical category-identity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species.

title: On Adaptive Step Sizes for Eligibility Traces in Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Many deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms store agent-environment interactions in a replay buffer and later learn by sampling transitions from it. However, this approach can be memory-inefficient and can delay learning because the agent can learn from a transition only when the buffer samples it. Additionally, most of these methods use one-step or short multi-step temporal-difference (TD) updates, which are slow at credit assignment. An alternative approach is to learn from the stream of observations as they arrive without relying on a buffer. Eligibility-trace algorithms allow these incremental updates and can also assign credit over many steps. These algorithms were common with linear function approximation but have only recently been used in deep RL. Basic questions, such as how to use vector step sizes with eligibility traces in the deep RL setting, remain open. In this work, we first show that adaptive vector step sizes must be part of the eligibility trace to keep the equivalence between the forward and backward views. We then show that the step sizes of common optimizers, such as Adam, do not have an online backward view. We introduce a new optimizer, Function-Space Distance (FSD), that maintains the forward-backward equivalence. We test four eligibility-trace algorithms covering semi-gradient and gradient TD updates, as well as value-based and actor-critic methods. We show that FSD performs better than SGD or naively applied Adam. The resulting algorithms outperform or match other streaming methods and are comparable to or better than PPO, which uses a buffer, in most environments. Code available at https://github.com/esraaelelimy/ada_traces

title: ClothCast: Generative Cloth World Modeling under Partial Observability
summary: World models support robotic manipulation by predicting how the scene evolves under a planned action. For garments this prediction is notoriously difficult: deformations are complex, and self-occlusion leaves much of the cloth unobserved. Planned gripper trajectories provide a useful motion prior because cloth held by a gripper moves with it, while the remaining deformation must be predicted.
