title: Evolutionary AI Control: Population-Level Safety Under Reproduction, Heredity, and Selection
summary: An AI agent can satisfy every individual safety check and still give rise to a population that violates a collective safety limit. This risk arises in open multi-agent systems, where agents copy themselves, modify their successors, and change system membership during a run. Selection then shifts the population toward traits outside the developers' optimization targets. We prove conditions under which safety guarantees persist through reproduction, inheritance, and selection, and we characterize how they fail. Four counterexamples illustrate these failures. Unauthorized copies, which violate a specified reproductive restriction, can each leave fewer than one successor on average while their expected number grows without bound under continued production from an expanding authorized population. Two lineages can each decline in isolation yet grow exponentially when they interact. Alternating between reproductive rules can drive growth even when each rule, applied alone, suppresses it. Selection can raise the population's average rate of unauthorized reproduction above a certified limit even though every agent's rate remains fixed. Whereas existing verification methods assume fixed or registered membership, we prove safety certificates, under stated assumptions, for populations whose agents create successors during a run. The main result bounds the expected cumulative harm over a run, including when a scheduler adapts the reproductive rules to the observed history. Further conditions cover every population state reachable through evolution and preserve reproductive restrictions as descendants inherit modifications. Drawing on the mechanisms by which multicellular organisms control cell reproduction, the framework enables developers to specify and verify these controls before deployment.

title: QASparse: Query-Adaptive Sparse Attention with Tailored Budgets and Tokens
summary: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.

title: RadioWorld: Transferring World Models to Radio-Frequency Radiance Fields
summary: Electromagnetic (EM) wave propagation in the physical world constitutes a Radio-Frequency (RF) radiance field, providing rich information for 6G communication and sensing. However, existing neural RF field methods suffer from three fundamental limitations: (1) they predominantly rely on per-scene optimization and cannot generalize to unseen scenes; (2) they require costly reference RF measurements in each target scene; and (3) they degrade severely when extrapolating beyond the vicinity of reference measurements. To overcome these limitations, we present RadioWorld, a general framework that adapts a world model to synthesize RF radiance fields directly from physical scene geometry and transceiver locations, without requiring any reference RF measurements at inference. Specifically, RadioWorld couples two specialized modules within a dual-stream Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture: a Scene-Understanding Transformer that encodes 3D scene geometry and transceiver locations to extract environment-aware global EM propagation features, and a Field-Generation Transformer that attends to these features to synthesize the RF radiance field with the local query conditions. We also establish UrbanRF-Bench, a large-scale ray-traced benchmark spanning 657 urban scenes and 32,850 RF radiance fields across seven global cities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RadioWorld significantly outperforms specialized baselines and accurately synthesizes RF fields at arbitrary locations in unseen cities. Code, datasets, and checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.

title: Controlled nonstationary G-diffusions: dynamic programming, weighted Harris contraction and entrance risk
summary: We study controlled nonstationary \(G\)-diffusions in a canonical-law formulation of covariance uncertainty. The principal structural result is an abstract weighted Harris--oscillation contraction theorem for translation-covariant nonlinear evolution families. A Lyapunov estimate for a dominating terminal-perturbation bound and a local space--time oscillation estimate for differences imply exponential contraction in a weighted quotient norm, without positive homogeneity, subadditivity or convexity. For elementary sample-and-hold feedback controls and a rectangular family of martingale laws, we construct a measurable controlled state map and prove deterministic- and stopped-time dynamic programming principles for the robust lower value. Under uniform ellipticity, differences of Bellman values belong to a common parabolic Pucci class; a local Harnack argument and an all-policy Lyapunov estimate verify the abstract hypotheses. For zero running cost, the contraction yields a unique tempered entrance nonlinear expectation and exponential attraction. With running cost, it yields a unique normalized nonstationary corrector and an additive cocycle, together with exponential convergence of relative values. Subtracting a scalar primitive of the cocycle gives an all-time viscosity solution of the backward Bellman--Isaacs equation. Autonomous and periodic coefficients yield additive eigenpairs, stationary and periodic ergodic equations, and convergence of long-time average costs. The results provide a long-time theory for optimally controlled dynamic risk evaluation under nonstationary covariance uncertainty.

title: MAWAM: Joint Imagination for Collaborative Robot Manipulation with a Multi-Agent World Action Model
summary: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.

title: AutoRPG: Harnessing Systematic AI for Non-Intrusive Low-Latency Mobile RPG Combat
summary: Automated combat in mobile RPGs plays a critical role in game quality assurance, requiring real-time behavior control that closely resembles human gameplay. However, existing approaches fail to satisfy these requirements, either because they lack fine-grained behavioral control or because they incur high inference latency. To address these challenges, we incorporate user gameplay experience to design AutoRPG, a systematic AI framework for automating mobile RPG combat. At a high level, AutoRPG decomposes the combat process into two stages: a high-level strategic planning phase that formulates the overall combat strategy, followed by a systematic execution phase powered by a suite of carefully designed lightweight modules encompassing target tracking, character movement, dodge maneuvering, and abnormal-state handling. Experiments on three popular mobile RPGs, i.e., Genshin Impact, Wuthering Waves, and Arknights: Endfield, demonstrate that AutoRPG consistently outperforms four competitive baselines across both combat quality and generalization capability, while behaving the most similarly to human players among all evaluated agents.

title: Relativising Integrity and Robustness: Prompt Injection and Partitioned Enclaves
summary: Relative security (RS) judges a system against a reference system, but has only been applied to confidentiality. We introduce relative integrity (RI), which states that every behaviour a system exhibits under an attacker's influence must be one the reference can exhibit for the same trusted inputs. RS and RI each choose their own reference runs, so together they accept attacks whose leak and effects the reference reproduces only in different runs. We therefore develop a further property, relative robustness (RR), which asks the same runs to reproduce both and is strictly stronger than RS and RI together. We give proof methods for RI and RR and a disproof method for RI, and apply them in two domains: (1) LLM agents under prompt injection, where the reference runs the same plan with a model that never obeys untrusted content, and (2) C programs partitioned across an SGX or TrustZone enclave boundary, where the reference keeps every function inside. We evaluate the properties on models of five published attacks, a support desk, an OP-TEE HOTP token and common agent defences. Two cases pass RS and RI but fail RR: an injection that makes the support desk's model accept any customer, as one input did in the Tensor Trust game, and the simulation step of the attack on Secret Network, in which an SGX enclave reveals a transfer's outcome without committing it. Our work is fully mechanised in Isabelle/HOL, with the enclave programs verified in C using AutoCorres2.

title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
summary: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.

title: Inferring Experimental Objectives in Microscopy Experiments from Decision Traces
summary: Modern microscopes can acquire, analyze and act on data far faster than human operators can decide what to measure next. Exploiting this speed in automated experiments requires the instrument to follow the scientific logic of the operator, and one way to encode that logic is through reward functions that become part of the operation process. Here we explore whether such reward functions can be learned from the decision histories of microscope operators. We propose multiple frameworks in which recorded choices among alternative measurement locations serve as comparative evidence about the operator's preferences, and we compare several algorithms for reconstructing the reward including interpretable linear models built on physically meaningful image descriptors, nonlinear functions of the same descriptors, an unsupervised image representation followed by preference modeling, and a preference trained deep kernel inspired model. The result of this analysis is a spatial field of reward functions over the sample that can be used to run the instrument. We also propose a way to benchmark these approaches, based on withheld decisions and on decision histories generated with known objectives. We then examine the possibility that a decision history contains changing priorities throughout the experiment. A hidden Markov model assigns distinct rewards to recurring selection strategies, whereas a continuous-state model tracks smoothly varying preference weights. Controlled sequences generated over real microscopy candidate sets show that both concealed switches and gradual drift can be recovered. These reward functions, learned directly from recorded decisions, provide candidate objectives for future automated microscopy experiments.

title: Contamination at the Operating Point: Train-Test Identity Overlap Inflates Low-FMR Face Recognition Accuracy by an Order of Magnitude
summary: Face verification systems are deployed by selecting a decision threshold that achieves a target false match rate (FMR); performance is then reported as the corresponding false non-match rate (FNMR). In practice, deployed systems operate at FMR $\le 10^{-6}$, but widely used benchmarks can share identities with the models' training corpora. Prior work (Wu et al., 2024) measures the resulting optimistic bias as a small additive change in 10-fold accuracy (up to 1.01 percentage points). We show that the bias is neither small nor constant: it is a multiplicative error that grows as FMR falls. First, we audit train-test overlap with a detector calibrated against a null distribution (rather than a hand-tuned threshold). Relative to WebFace42M, we flag 88.6% of MS1MV3 identities and 14.3% of IJB-C subjects as present, despite WebFace260M's published de-overlap explicitly naming IJB-C. Manual review of 100 flagged IJB-C subjects confirms 69.2%, implying a residual overlap of roughly 9.9%. Second, holding the model fixed, removing only the contaminated identities from the test set increases FNMR by 3.6$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-4}$, 6.3$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-5}$, and 13.9$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-6}$, while a same-size random removal does not. The effect is traced to a shorter impostor tail that lowers the threshold. The magnitude of the shift depends on the training corpus and does not cancel betweent margin between our model and a publicbaseline by half. Third, we give the first direct measurement of the effective number of independent impostor comparisons in IJB-C: only 2.7 million effectively independent comparisons at FMR=$10^{-6}$, which is below all commonly accepted reporting rules. Finallyth a known training corpus, we build areal-face protocol with audited zero overlap that resolves FMR=$10^{-8}$.

title: What Makes Recurrence Generalize Across Lengths?
summary: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.

title: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training
summary: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning data and chosen so that exposure disagreed with FPR alone or propensity alone, exposure named the first exploited pattern and its onset window in all six runs. Exploitation occurred only on hard prompts, where an accepted exploit gets a large group-normalized advantage. Auditing exposure before RL therefore identifies the loophole a policy will likely exploit first.

title: But Can You Draw It Live? The Emergence of AI Duidus for Adjudicating Suspected Generative AI Use in Digital Art Commission Communities
summary: Generative AI poses new challenges for digital art commission communities, where a commission's value often depends on human labor and authorship. We examine a novel community-developed dispute resolution mechanism called an AI duidu, or livestreamed drawing bet, used when an artist is suspected of using generative AI. In an AI duidu, an accuser challenges an artist to create a new artwork live, and community members vote on whether the artist created the disputed artwork without AI assistance. Often, both parties stake money with an intermediary, who releases it after the vote. Through interviews with 17 accusers, accused artists, or intermediaries, we examined how the AI duidu emerged and how participants perceived its effectiveness and risks. We found that AI duidus shift authorship verification from the artwork itself to the artist, using livestreamed creative labor, community adjudication, and wagering to establish provenance and negotiate community norms surrounding AI use.

title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT
summary: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.

title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
summary: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). The transforms, audits and raw records are available from the authors.

title: Compared to What? Calibrating Machine-Unlearning Diagnostics with Present, Absent and Suppressed Anchors
summary: Unlearning methods for language models are judged mainly by behaviour, but a model can stop producing an answer while still encoding it. Internal diagnostics such as linear probes, the logit lens and relearning speed are used to tell removal from suppression, yet none has been checked against cases where the answer is known. We build such cases. A present anchor learned a set of synthetic facts; an absent anchor is a never-taught oracle retrained without them; and suppressed anchors are unlearned with their lower layers frozen, so the facts stay encoded below the frozen block by construction. We compare these anchors with NPO, RMU and gradient difference at a matched operating point on GPT-2 Small and Qwen3-0.6B-Base, scoring every diagnostic per entity with AUROC against the oracle. Behaviour cannot separate the suppressed anchors from the oracle (AUROC 0.51 to 0.58), while probes, the logit lens and relearning gain can (0.65 to 1.00), and the oracle seeds stay near 0.5. Applied to NPO on both models and RMU on Qwen3, the validated diagnostics disagree: probes put the facts at the oracle's level, while the models still relearn them much faster than a never-taught model does. Every unlearned model, anchor or method, also assigns the forgotten answer a far lower log-probability than the oracle does, a black-box signal that flagged all of them. A drift-ratio specificity rule fails on known cases. Code, data and every run are at https://github.com/ArsalanKaleem/unlearning-audit.

title: Seeing Beyond Names: Image-Grounded Concept Linking for Robust Vision-Language Recognition
summary: A zero-shot vision-language classifier is highly sensitive to the class names it receives. Even when images remain unchanged, replacing familiar labels with synonyms, abbreviations, or ontology terms can significantly alter predictions. We investigate this \emph{vocabulary shift} using a leakage-free evaluation protocol across Tiny ImageNet, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetV2. With CLIP ViT-B/16, alternative class names reduce top-1 accuracy by $14.8$--$17.6$ percentage points. To address this issue, we propose \emph{image-grounded concept linking}, a training-free method that maps class names to visual concepts and uses a reliability gate to improve predictions. The method outperforms a template ensemble across all four datasets, achieving a pooled gain of $1.8$ points. We further evaluate five vision-language backbones across four datasets. Our method improves performance in $16$ of $20$ backbone--dataset combinations, with no significantly negative results. It also reduces pooled negative log-likelihood across all five backbones. Stronger text linking and transductive refinement provide no consistent improvements, suggesting that accurate visual class-name linking remains the main challenge. A second CLIP ViT-B/16 seed confirms the improvement on ImageNetV2, but not on ImageNet-A.

title: Latent-Predisposition Personas for Heterogeneous and Reliable LLM Survey Simulation
summary: LLM personas are used to simulate survey publics, which should reproduce not only answer distributions but also within-person coherence and stability. Drawing on mass belief systems research, we show that persona-conditioned LLMs produce over-constrained publics. Across three model families and three U.S. surveys, opinions on unrelated issues are 1.6-4.6 times as correlated as among humans, and party identification explains 2.5-7.6 times as much answer variance. Common remedies (temperature, diversity instructions, backstories) weaken these correlations by making answers more random. On Qwen, their ten-day test-retest reliability falls to 33-59% of the human level, and when made consistent they lose correlation fit. We propose Latent-Predisposition Personas (LPP), whose persons differ stably, not randomly. Each persona receives political engagement, value priorities, and party-relative issue deviations that grow as engagement falls. Answers are sharpened and calibrated to toplines and party crosstabs. At selected operating points, LPP is never significantly worse than any baseline and far more reliable. At matched human-level reliability, it has the lowest correlation error in all six model-survey combinations, also at a lower target. Errors still exceed those between human samples, and gains on framing effects and a frontier closed model are partial.

title: Who Sent It or How It Moved? Sender Shortcuts in Cryptocurrency Anti-Money-Laundering Benchmarks, Audited on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++
summary: Two public benchmarks dominate graph-based anti-money-laundering (AML) research on Bitcoin: the transaction-level Elliptic dataset, extended as Elliptic++, and the subgraph-level Elliptic2. In both, a label is assigned according to the entity that sends the funds. We ask whether models trained on these benchmarks learn how laundering moves or merely who sent the money, and we propose a diagnostic protocol to tell the two apart: a sender lookup baseline, a novelty baseline, a sender-disjoint split with a leakage check, and a decomposition of performance into sender, receiver and intrinsic signal. On Elliptic2 the task largely reduces to classifying the sender. Under the standard random split, a no-learning lookup of sender history reaches a PR-AUC of 0.954, against 0.975 for gradient boosting on 456 features; our reimplementation of RevClassify reproduces its reported 0.97 and falls to 0.126 without sender information. When senders are held out, performance drops to 0.746, and the subgraph's own structure, transactions and receivers fall from 0.619 to 0.186. On Elliptic++ the same protocol finds the shortcut negligible: sender history reaches only 0.340 against 0.986 for the full model (3.5 against 10.1 times the test prevalence), adding it to the full model raises PR-AUC by less than 0.004 in every seed, and the transaction's own features keep 0.883 when sending addresses are held out. We trace the difference to the unit of sender identity: Elliptic2 senders are entity clusters that recur across many labeled subgraphs, whereas Elliptic++ senders are individual addresses, and fewer than half of test transactions have a sending address seen in training. A shared sender-based label rule thus produces a severe shortcut in one benchmark and a negligible one in the other, so the diagnostic must be run on each benchmark.

title: ParseGap: Testing What Coding Agents Authorize and What Shells Execute
summary: LLM coding agents authorize shell commands by parsing a command string against a policy and passing the raw string to a system shell, so the gate adjudicates one reading while the shell executes another. We present ParseGap, a differential testing framework that runs each command through an unmodified vendor checker and GNU Bash 5.2 in an isolated container, flagging a violation whenever an approved command produces policy-violating runtime effects. Across eight production coding agents, ParseGap identifies 17 root causes across three divergence boundaries: at the parse, where an upstream tree-sitter-bash defect hides a second command from Mistral Vibe and Gemini CLI; at the utility, where every checker permits read-only binaries whose arguments write files or launch programs (9-47 of 55 cases); and at confinement, where an allow rule in OpenAI Codex CLI disables its read-only OS sandbox. Live trials across two frontier models triggered policy violations in all 16 agent-model pairs (14 under configured restrictions). To eliminate the second reading, we design ShellPlan, which compiles a strict Bash subset once into a typed execution plan, validates utility arguments against positive capability specifications, and dispatches approved plans directly via execve without a shell. Over a formal operational model, we prove single-interpretation dispatch and bound touched programs and files under audited assumptions. ShellPlan admitted 0/4,174 active attacks across six static suites and 0/90 hits in a ten-model agent benchmark (62/90 unguarded) at 1.28 ms median gate latency, preserving 36/36 (100%) frontier standard-dev completion (74/100 overall) and 0/348 external over-allows outside modeled exceptions.

title: When Does Decomposition Help? Empirical Study on Workload-Architecture Affinity in LLM Inference Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference can be organized as independent monolithic replicas, tensor- or pipeline-parallel serving groups, or disaggregated prefill and decode services. Although decomposition is often presented as a route to higher efficiency, its benefit depends on workload shape, model fit, and whether phase-specific resources can be independently scaled. Existing comparisons frequently change several of these factors at once. We isolate the architectural effect by evaluating five SGLang serving organizations under the same four-A100-40GB hardware envelope, pinned Qwen3-8B model, software stack, prompts, and arrival schedules. Our evaluation contains 150 audited conditions over short-chat, decode-heavy, and 32K prefill-heavy workloads. Four independent one-GPU replicas achieve the lowest end-to-end latency for short chat and long output and are the only architecture stable in every condition. Pipeline parallelism reduces 32K time to first token by 58-59% at non-stress rates, while hybrid pipeline-based disaggregation achieves the best 32K end-to-end latency at 0.4 requests/s. In contrast, B's single-VM static TP2+TP2 split, without independent phase scaling, does not improve tested latency over replication and collapses at higher 32K load. These results reveal a workload-architecture affinity: pipeline decomposition favors prefill-heavy computation, whereas replication favors decode-heavy and concurrent traffic. More broadly, decomposition is not a monotonic optimization; its value depends on matching parallelism granularity to the dominant phase and preserving queue stability.

title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
summary: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.

title: DriveTTO: Understanding Search and Selection in Test-Time Trajectory Optimization for End-to-End Driving
summary: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.

title: Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
summary: The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.

title: BQDNA: Multi-Head Binary Spherical Quantization for Genomic Sequence Modeling
summary: Decoding biological information from long, repetitive DNA remains challenging. Genomic language models (gLMs) often follow the conventional language-model pretrain-and-adapt paradigm. However, the lack of inherent semantic segmentation and prior rules makes hand-crafted tokenizers like k-mer and BPE suboptimal. We introduce context-aware \textbf{BQVAE} for scalar quantization of DNA and \textbf{BQDNA}, an autoregressive gLM supporting multi-head codebooks. Comprehensive experiments reveal that: (1) unique training dynamics of vector quantization in DNA space, including the importance of alignment between training corpus and downstream data. (2) superior performance of BQVAE over hand-crafted tokenizers and vanilla VQVAE. (3) remarkable cross-species generalization capability of BQDNA, which achieves state-of-the-art performance with merely 0.1B multi-species training for BQVAE and 1 epoch training on hg38 for BQDNA, outperforming gLMs pretrained with 10$\sim$100x more tokens. Our findings underscore the potential of learned vector quantization for genomic sequence representation. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/BQDNA

title: Seeing vs. Knowing: Counterfactual Supervision and Correction for 3D-Aware Object Editing
summary: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.
